label: copy-phase input token p (fed back after the first copy output)
explanation: Fires only in the copy phase when the token being fed back as input is p, provided it is not the very first copied token (recall_idx >= 2, i.e. the p is original token 1 or later). Never fires in the original phase, on <DEL>, or on any other input token (only 7 of 75k activations are on a non-p input). When p is original token 0 and is fed back at the first copy step (recall_idx 1), it fires rarely and weakly. It fires at a near-constant rate of about 3.3% of all copy-phase steps from recall_idx 2 on, with no dependence on what is being output or on the previous token. From the examples, magnitude is lowest when p is original token 1 (around 0.55 of max), higher at later positions (0.75 to 1.0 of max), and somewhat lower on the second of two consecutive p inputs.

issues: None of the claims could be refuted. Test score for the predicate: precision 1.0, recall 0.985, F1 0.993, mass recall 0.9995. There are 0 false positives on test.

All 1103 test misses fall in one class: p fed back at recall_idx 1, i.e. p was original token 0 and is the first copy input. Activations there are tiny (0.01 to 0.05 of max) and hold 0.1% of the activation mass. This matches the explanation's 'fires rarely and weakly'. Scored on its own, recall_idx==1 with p as input gives precision 0.066, so it is right to leave it out.

The other factual claims check out on dev. The feature never fires in the original phase or on <DEL> (0 activations in each). Only 7 dev activations have an input other than p (n:4, l:2, v:1). The rate is flat at about 0.033 for recall_idx 2 through 8, and it is uniform across output tokens and previous tokens.

Minor caveat: the magnitude claims (lowest when p is original token 1, lower on the second of two p's in a row) were not measured separately, and the explanation says so itself. One example from misses fits: 'p p h 3 <DEL> p [p:0.67]'.
